title: Multiplexing of Continuous-Variable and Discrete-Variable Quantum Key Distribution Systems over Fibered and Free-Space Channels
authors: Mattia Sabatini, Edoardo Rossi, Matías R. Bolaños, Francesco Vedovato, Thomas Liege, Eleni Diamanti, Giuseppe Vallone, Paolo Villoresi, Yoann Piétri, Marco Avesani
abstract: Future quantum communication infrastructures will need to serve heterogeneous users on shared physical channels: short-range, high-throughput links favor Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution (CV-QKD), while long-reach, high-loss links remain the domain of Discrete-Variable QKD (DV-QKD). Wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) of the two protocols on a common channel would address both regimes simultaneously, but their markedly different noise sensitivities make coexistence non-trivial and, to date, experimentally untested. Here we report the first simultaneous operation of two independent CV- and DV-QKD systems on a common optical channel, using standard C-band DWDM filters at 1550.12 nm (CV) and 1545.32 nm (DV). We demonstrate joint operation on both optical fiber and a 620 m urban daylight free-space link. On fiber, the two systems exhibit the expected complementarity, crossing over at 7.56 dB of channel loss where both deliver $\sim$1.43 Mbit/s; in daylight free-space, both sustain Mbit/s key rates under time-varying atmospheric attenuation. Across all configurations we observe no measurable multiplexing-induced penalty in QBER or excess noise. These results establish hybrid CV-DV WDM as a practical building block for heterogeneous quantum communication networks, where metropolitan high-throughput users and long-reach backbone links can be served on a single physical infrastructure.
summary: This paper reports the first experimental demonstration of multiplexing CV-QKD and DV-QKD systems onto a single optical channel using WDM. By testing the setup over both fiber and free-space links, the authors prove that the two protocols can operate simultaneously without performance degradation. This establishes a practical, hybrid building block for future heterogeneous quantum communication networks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for a practical building block to serve heterogeneous quantum communication networks by simultaneously operating Continuous-Variable (CV) and Discrete-Variable (DV) Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) systems over a shared physical channel.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the first simultaneous operation of independent CV-QKD and DV-QKD systems on a common optical link, showing no measurable multiplexing-induced penalty.
method: They utilized Wavelength-Division Multiplexing (WDM) to combine the two protocols, testing the setup over both optical fiber and a 620 m urban daylight free-space link.
model_or_system: The system involves two distinct QKD protocols: CV-QKD using Gaussian-modulated coherent states and DV-QKD using the three-state one-decoy BB84 protocol. The transmission occurs over a shared channel, tested in both fiber and free-space environments.
key_observables: Secret Key Rate (SKR), Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), and excess noise, measured across varying channel losses.
important_parameters: The systems operate at distinct C-band wavelengths (1550.12 nm for CV and 1545.32 nm for DV), and performance is analyzed across channel losses, showing a crossover point at 7.56 dB on fiber.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the WDM approach can support coexistence despite the protocols' different noise sensitivities, which was experimentally verified by observing no penalty.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setups for both CV-QKD and DV-QKD, and later figures show the time evolution of the multiplexed SKR versus time during free-space operation.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup, first demonstrating the feasibility of joint operation on both fiber and free-space links, and concludes by establishing the hybrid CV-DV WDM approach as a practical network component.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum networks, specifically addressing the engineering challenge of integrating different quantum communication modalities (CV vs. DV) onto shared physical infrastructure.

Figure 4. Schematic of the multiplexed DV-QKD and CV- QKD setup. The CV transmitter (Alice CV) and receiver (Bob CV) are located in room 1, while the DV transmitter (Alice DV) and receiver (Bob DV) are located in room 2. At the transmitter side, the optical outputs of Alice DV and Alice CV are combined by a 100 GHz DWDM and launched into a common quantum channel, implemented either as a 20 km single-mode fiber spool or as a variable-loss link using an electronically controlled VOA. At the receiver side, a sec- ond DWDM with identical specifications demultiplexes the two wavelengths and routes them to Bob CV and Bob DV, respectively.
